image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Bar chart / histogram-like time series with yearly bars.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **separate grouped time segments** along a shared horizontal timeline for different wars.
   - Includes **overlapping bars** for the Iraq and Afghanistan periods, distinguished by color.
   - No faceting into separate panels; labels for wars are placed beneath the corresponding time ranges.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Number of front-page war-related headlines | Quantitative | Bar height / position on y-axis |
| War / conflict (WWI, WWII, Korea, Vietnam, Gulf, Afghanistan, Iraq) | Categorical/nominal | Horizontal grouping by time range, text labels beneath chart, color for overlapping recent wars |
| Iraq vs. Afghanistan distinction | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (gray vs. muted green) |

comments.raw_comment: This is a bar graph showing the yearly war-related front-page headlines. I notice that as time has gone on, for the most part, front-page headlines that are war-related have gone down and were at their peak in WW1. I wonder why this is. I notice that most war headlines usually are at their height in the middle of the war as opposed to the beginning of the end which is surprising to me because I would think that the announcement of a war beginning or ending would make a lot of headlines.  Title:War-Related Headlines Take a Back Seat

Many young people (younger than 12 years old) aren’t aware that we are at war, and have been since before most of them were born. This, alongside the graph shows a change in America towards not only our ignorance of war and its atrocities, but our indifference to it, and that is more horrifying than any war crime.

Another thing I noticed was that remote regional wars, such as in Vietnam and Iraq, had much less coverage. This may be because of the disinterest of the American people in wars that don't affect them or seem far away because WWI & WWII both have much more headlines than recent wars.

Finally, I noticed that at a similar time to when the Vietnam draft occurred, the coverage decreased. This could be due to the fact that people do not want to read about the danger their sons and husbands are undergoing. Another idea that is people dislike the draft and want to pull out, influencing the media to talking about the war less. 

Some things I wondered about was what factors resulted in the Iraq war being covered more than the Afghanistan war and what this graph would look like fro sources other than the New York Times.

comments.raw_comment: Many headlines were made for what was originally known as the Great War, a war that for the first time ever was on a global scale. Many newspaper and reports were made on this war, as the world was shook by this terrifying war that lasted for 4 years. As the years passed though, many more wars occurred, and there was even another second World War. But as the years passed, there became less headlines. But why is that? Is there a lack of interest in wars? The truth is, they're just not put on the front covers as headlines that much. In fact, a lot of information on these wars could be recorded on something of recent innovations: social media and the internet. The internet is a vast source of knowledge and communications, and is a great way for the younger generations to discuss and create content. An example would be in January, at the start of 2020. Many memes on World War 3 was being made, and all of them were mainly put on social media. The ease to record and talk about these issues, making them a big topic of discussion, doesn't have to be covered on the headlines of big newspaper to gain lots of attention. So it makes sense as to why there's a lack of headlines on these wars.

We can notice that the number of New York Times front-page articles of wars has been largely decreasing since World War I. Another interesting trend is that as wars go on, the later years of the war start to receive less coverage by the New York Times; the majority of the graphs are skewed right. 

The most pressing question is why the number of war-related front-page headlines has largely been decreasing over the past century. One answer could be that as society has industrialized and modernized, more issues have started coming into focus in our society -- for instance, the coronavirus today or global warming may be taking away from war coverage. Regardless, the impact of this graph and it's conclusions is profound, because media is the way most people get their information, and understanding how our media describes events differently is pivotal for us in shaping the way our society thinks.

comments.raw_comment: This graph shows how many New York Times front page headlines involved certain wars over a number of years. These wars include World War 1 and 2, the Korean, Vietnam, and Gulf Wars, and the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. WWI had the highest number of headlines, which was over 75. On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the article that included these visual representations and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

The next “What’s Going On in This Graph?” will be released in two days – Friday, March 13 with moderation on Wednesday, March 18.  The topic – teen problems.  Stay tuned.
